newsitem.title: INDONESIA: ACPC should consider consumers' interest-Indonesia.
newsitem.headline: ACPC should consider consumers' interest-Indonesia.

text.p: Indonesia said on Wednesday that the Association of Coffee Producing Countries' (ACPC) technical committee meeting next week would discuss the surge in coffee prices and premium of arabica over robusta.
Paian Nainggolan, Indonesia's representative to the ACPC, also said it would be timely for the grouping to demonstrate it was not a cartel by considering the interests of consumers.
"The ACPC should demonstrate it is not a cartel that only takes into account the interests of producers," he told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"The organisation should demonstrate it would also take into account the interests of consumers," he said.
Nainggolan said coffee prices were becoming "uncontrollable" due to speculative and fund buying.
"The meeting is expected to review the Rio decision," Nainggolan said. "It is also likely to discuss the difference in the price of robusta and arabica."
"We don't know how we will deal with the difference in prices between arabica and robusta, but I think the issue will be raised by African producers at the meeting," he said.
The 14-member ACPC decided at its meeting in Brazil in late January to reduce exports of robusta by one million 60-kg bags, and arabica by 300,000 bags in the first six months of 1997.
Coffee prices have doubled since November on worries over lower supplies from Central America and Brazil this year, along with transport and grower strikes in Colombia.
The supply tightness, and steady demand from roasters, was expected to keep coffee prices underpinned.

In response, leading coffee roasters such as Folgers Coffee Co and Maxwell House have raised their prices by a minimum of 20 percent, and U.S. industry analysts have said that price hikes are usually accompanied by a decline in consumption.
The ACPC technical committee, which is scheduled to meet on March 20 in London, links Brazil, Colombia, Indonesia, El Salvador, the Ivory Coast and Uganda.
Indonesia, Asia's sole ACPC member, is the biggest producer after Brazil and Colombia.
Nainggolan said he expected African producers to raise the issue of the price premium of arabica over robusta since their economies depended heavily on coffee as an export earner.
He said the meeting was expected to be chaired by ACPC president, Rubens Barbosa, and that the policy-making ACPC council would meet in May.
Nainggolan said Indonesia would not be making any specific proposals at the technical committee meeting.
